cia-0000124276: A January 1958 CIA item lists Soviet stations for watching artificial earth satellites by eye, with their map coordinates, drawn up for the International Geophysical Year. cia-0000126876: An August 1968 CIA report surveys how the world's communist parties reacted to the invasion of Czechoslovakia. cia-0000126976: Dated October 1975, this CIA Weekly Summary covers Angola after independence, a companion to the Weekly Review's treatment of the same subject that month. cia-0000132276:

cia-0000134276: Strain across the Caribbean that would not lift fills a CIA paper dated November 3, 1959. Ten months into the revolution, the neighborhood had yet to calm down. cia-0000136276: A cable dated 1 May 1954 is among the declassified CIA papers on the need for consolidation phase policy plans, planning for the day after the victory. cia-0000139476: Father Lawrence Jenco's second debriefing leads this task force report. It covers 9-15 August 1986. Jenco was a released hostage. un-ga-res-a-69-76:
The world's sole forum for arms talks gets a review in Resolution A/69/76, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Conference on Disarmament, based in Geneva, holds the prime role in hard talks on arms cuts. The Assembly had the conference's own report before it. Word from the Secretary-General, and speeches by foreign chiefs, had each voiced both support for the body and worry at its stall.

Real talks on firm points are needed, the text holds, and the state of the world should give them fresh push. Yet worry runs deep: for all the hard work of its member states, the conference had long failed to agree a plan of work. That deadlock, unbroken for years, hangs over the whole text.
un-ga-res-376:
Korea's division hardened into war, and Resolution 376, adopted by the General Assembly on 7 October 1950, restates the UN aim. Past votes of 1947, 1948, and 1949 had set the goal: a free, united Korea. The UN Commission on Korea had now reported. The goals, the text admits, had not been met. Worse, an armed attack from North Korea had tried to wipe out the Republic of Korea by force.

The Assembly recalls its 1948 ruling on the south. A lawful state, the Government of the Republic of Korea, held real rule over the part of Korea the UN team could reach. That state rested on votes the team had watched. The text holds to the goal of one Korea, free of outside force.
un-sc-res-76: A wire from Batavia is passed on in Security Council Resolution 76, passed on 5 October 1949. The Consular Commission at Batavia had cabled the Council's president on 5 August. It asked that the United Nations take over the future costs of the armed watchers in Indonesia, the men who kept eye on the truce between Dutch and Indonesian forces. The Council rules, in full, that the wire be sent to the Secretary-General.
un-sc-res-276: Within the United Nations official record, Resolution 276 is the Security Council text catalogued for 1970. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-676: Kept in the official record of the United Nations, Security Council Resolution 676 is catalogued here as dating from 1990. un-sc-res-1476: Adopted in 2003, Resolution 1476 adds one more entry to the Security Council's long numbered run. The copy here is transcribed from the official record on English Wikisource. un-sc-res-1676: Resolution 1676 is a formal Security Council text held here through a Wikisource copy of the official record. cia-0000132776:
Regional fear shapes this CIA paper on Cuba and the Caribbean, dated August 4, 1960. Castro's example, analysts worried, was spreading encouragement to movements across the islands and coasts nearby. Washington watched Cuba's neighbors almost as closely as Cuba itself.

The Caribbean framing returns here after appearing in the spring papers, now with exile training under way. The briefing treats one revolution as a possible spark for others, the core Cold War fear in the hemisphere. Its declassified text, held through the CIA Reading Room mirror, preserves that worry in the language of the time.

The brigade of Cuban exiles was training that fall for the landing it would make in April 1961. The catalog record for this item is minimal, with no subject or author stated. cia-0000136676: A document in Spanish dated 4 February 1961, held in the CIA's declassified 2506 Brigade files. un-sc-res-176:
Security Council Resolution 176, adopted on October 4, 1962, recommended Algeria for membership in the United Nations. Algeria had won independence from France that July, after a war of eight years that shook both lands and killed vast numbers of people. A seat at the UN marked the new state's arrival on the world stage in formal terms.

The General Assembly admitted Algeria four days after the council acted. Few admissions carried such weight: France had long claimed Algeria was part of France itself, not a colony. The short resolution thus sealed a verdict that the war had already rendered, and Algeria soon became a leading voice for other peoples still under colonial rule.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d76: On October 30, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, the day the Moscow Conference formally ended. His message is Document 76 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. London had its own reading of the Moscow results, and the prime minister kept his channel to Washington warm as ever. The record gives the date and the names and nothing narrower. The message is printed in the Foreign Relations series with the day's other traffic.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d176: A third Roosevelt letter to Hull dated October 30, 1943 in the Moscow section stands as Document 176 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Repetition at this scale marks a day when much had to be settled at a distance: results weighed, thanks sent, and next steps set. The record gives the parties and the date and no subject. The letter is part of the Foreign Relations series' Moscow record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d276:
A secret memorandum of conversation at Cairo on 26 November 1943 records a meeting at half past eleven that morning. American and British information and public relations officers settled how conference photographs and films would be handled. Army colonels sit alongside staff of the British and American information services.

The agreed rules are practical. Each side processes its own still photographs in Cairo under security conditions and exchanges material. American film goes unprocessed to Washington, while British film is processed in Cairo. No picture of any kind may be released before the final release date, given the secrecy of the Tehran leg. All conference pictures, still and moving, are pooled for every party and carry one credit line: United Nations Photographic Pool.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d376:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record a luncheon at Tehran on 1 December 1943, at one in the afternoon, dominated by the planned meeting with Turkey's president. The text of a telegram inviting President Inönü to Cairo for 3, 4, or 5 December was discussed and agreed.

Hopkins insists the allies must first settle exactly what military help Turkey would get if she entered the war. Churchill's offer stands at twenty squadrons, mostly fighters, and three anti-aircraft regiments, with no land forces and no promises beyond that. His prize would be Turkish air bases for steady bombing of the Ploesti oil fields, and he wants landing craft only for a temporary Rhodes assault in March. Roosevelt, caught between the Italian, French, and Overlord demands on the same craft, asks for military advice before anything is sandwiched in.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d476:
On December 4, 1943, the opening day of the Second Cairo Conference, the Combined Chiefs of Staff sent a message to General Dwight D. Eisenhower at Allied Force Headquarters. Eisenhower then commanded Allied forces in the Mediterranean, based in North Africa. The State Department printed the chiefs' message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Traffic from the Combined Chiefs to a theater commander carried the alliance's decisions out of the conference room and into the field. Eisenhower stood at the receiving end of Cairo's choices about where Allied strength would go next. For readers, the message marks the point where summit strategy began turning into orders for the armies.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d576:
J. Leighton Stuart, the American ambassador to China, wrote to Secretary of State George C. Marshall on September 24, 1948. Stuart, a missionary educator born in China, was the last American ambassador to serve the Nationalist government on the mainland. His report is the final document in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

By September 1948 the Chinese Communists were winning the civil war, and the China that the Cairo Declaration had promised so much was disappearing. An editor's choice to end the volume here is pointed: the story that began with Chiang at Cairo closes with his government's collapse. For readers, Stuart's report is a somber bookend to the whole record.
frus-1944-quebec-d76:
James W. Riddleberger wrote to Harry Hopkins on September 1, 1944. Riddleberger headed the Division of Central European Affairs. Hopkins served as President Roosevelt's special assistant and closest aide. The State Department printed the letter in the Quebec 1944 volume.

Central European questions sat near the heart of the Quebec agenda. Germany's defeat raised hard choices about occupation and borders. A division chief writing to Hopkins put expert views near the President. For readers, the letter shows how regional knowledge reached the summit's inner circle. It arrived eleven days before the conference opened.
frus-1944-quebec-d176:
No official account survives of the dinner meeting on September 12, 1944, at the Governor General's residence. The editors reconstruct it from General Arnold's memoir. Messages from the Russians and from Harriman about the Polish patriots in Warsaw had arrived, and aid to Poland came up at the table. Marshall and Arnold talked the problem over at length.

Arnold records that helping Warsaw was a large problem never completely solved. Churchill also produced new ideas about winning the war: getting more British planes, ships, and soldiers into the final battle against Japan. Arnold answered that the Pacific lacked land masses for Europe's heavy bomber fleets. Even 1,500 of 3,500 bombers would be lucky to be usable, and B-29s were preferred anyway.
frus-1944-quebec-d276:
Somervell and Leathers, the American and British transport chiefs, reported on September 15, 1944, on the personnel movement problem after Germany's defeat. Their appendices size the task for the first year, assuming Germany fell on October 1. American operational movements alone totaled about 3.6 million men, including replacements, build-up, and redeployment for the war against Japan, plus 1.7 million for demobilization and repatriation.

British operational movements came to about 2.1 million, with nearly a million more to demobilize or repatriate. A precise analysis, the authors warn, was impossible until combined agencies studied the problem against the chiefs' strategy decisions. They recommended the Combined Administrative Committee take it up with the planners, the transportation committee, and the shipping authorities.

Volume one of four sets the scene before Hernan Cortes lands. It describes the Aztec empire at its height, ruled by Montezuma from Tenochtitlan, a great lake city of temples, markets, and canals.

Prescott explains Aztec government, religion, warfare, and daily life in detail drawn from Spanish and native sources. He writes history in the manner of a novel, with vivid scenes and strong characters. Readers get both a rich portrait of a lost civilization and the background they need for the clash that follows in later volumes.
tob-4146-15476:
Books eight through twelve fill volume three of Ganguli's Mahabharata, and the war burns toward its end. Great champions fall one by one. A night attack slaughters sleeping warriors, an act the epic itself treats as shameful. Victory, when it comes, tastes of ash.

Widows mourn on the field, funerals follow, and Yudhishthira, the eldest Pandava, takes the throne with a heavy heart. Long talks on duty and grief slow the pace on purpose. The epic turns from deeds of war to their cost. Ganguli's steady translation lets the sorrow build, page after page, without relief.
tob-9052-15476:
Grief rules volume three of Ganguli's Mahabharata, as the war of Kurukshetra ends. The field lies covered with the dead of both houses. Widows and mothers search the corpses, and the victors find their crown brings no joy.

Funeral rites, laments, and hard reckonings take the place of battles. The epic turns, by design, from action to mourning and reflection on what violence costs. Yudhishthira rules a kingdom of ashes and doubts his own part in winning it. Ganguli carries the slow, somber books with patience. Readers feel the full weight the Sanskrit poem places on victory.
tob-13329-15476:
Books eight to twelve form volume three of Ganguli's Mahabharata, the epic's dark second half. The great battle grinds to its end as champion after champion dies. A shameful night raid kills the last sleeping warriors of the beaten side.

Aftermath fills the rest: grief on the field, funeral fires, and the slow, unwilling work of rule. Yudhishthira must be coaxed to govern the kingdom he has won at such cost. Long discourses on duty replace the clash of arms. Ganguli's translation turns elegiac with the poem itself. Seldom has a war story spent so much strength on sorrow.

Edmund T. Whittaker wrote the classic history of how physicists explained light and electricity before Einstein. His subject runs from Descartes, who filled space with spinning whirlpools of fine matter, to the aether theories of the Victorian age. Maxwell's equations and the discovery of the electron close the long story.

Whittaker was a working mathematician who lived through the upheaval he describes, and it shows in his grasp of detail. Generations of students have treated the book as the standard history of field theory. It also reminds readers that the aether, now discarded, once organized the best science of its century.
tob-4176:
Teresa of Avila, the Spanish nun and reformer, described the soul as a crystal castle in The Interior Castle, her mature masterpiece of 1577. Benedict Zimmerman translated her guide for English readers. Seven sets of mansions lead inward, room by room, toward the King who waits at the center.

Each mansion marks a stage of prayer, from stumbling effort to quiet union. Teresa writes from her own trials, with humor about distractions and dry spells that still disarms readers. Nuns under her rule received the book first; the world claimed it next. Many judges call it the greatest guide to the life of prayer ever written.
tob-9776: A. J. Maas wrote this Catholic Encyclopedia article on the Hexaemeron, the six days of creation described in the first chapter of Genesis. It sums up how early Church writers and later theologians read those six days, whether as plain days, ages, or figures of speech. Maas writes as a scholar for general readers who need a clear map of a long debate. Short and factual, the piece works as a starting point on how Christians have understood the creation story.
burton-two-trips-to-gorilla-land-1876:
Richard Burton, the boldest traveler of his age, went after the gorilla in 1876. Two Trips to Gorilla Land and the Cataracts of the Congo tells his search in Gabon. Burton had crossed Africa and Arabia; the great ape still drew him on.

He tells of rivers, trade, fevers, and the falls of the Congo, with the gorilla as his grail. His pen is dry, learned, and full of the lore of the coast. The book adds his great name to the gorilla shelf of his century. Few explorers wrote with his mix of grit and wit.
britten-art-magic-1876:
Emma Hardinge Britten said a sage's ghost taught her the lore in Art Magic, her dense tract of 1876. The ghost bears the name Cheval Louis de B. Through her hand he maps the schools, rites, and laws of the occult from old Egypt to her own day.

Ranks of spirits, charms, and the risks of rite fill the book. Britten casts it as fact, not tale. Groups in the United States took it as a core text of rite. It is a ground stone of magic in that land. Britten had a flair for the grand claim, and she backs it here with dense lore. Fans must sift her zeal from her facts with care.
britten-ghost-land-1876:
Tales of hunts for truth in far lands fill Ghost Land, Emma Hardinge Britten's book of 1876. It is the mate to her Art Magic of the same year. Britten tracks adepts, bands, and marvels through Europe and past it. She writes as one who claims to have seen much at first hand.

Ghost lore here mixes trek tale with creed. Dark rooms, odd cures, and bands with hid names crowd the pages. Britten kept the teller's name hid at first print. The pair of books maps the hid world she claimed to know. Her claims drew both faith and scorn in her own day. That split still marks the book, which fans read as trek tale and creed at once.
maskelyne-modern-spiritualism-1876:
John Nevil Maskelyne shows the tricks of the dark room in Modern Spiritualism, his bust book of 1876. Maskelyne was the top stage mage of London. He and his mate built a famed hall of feats. Seers, he says, use the same craft: hid ropes, false hands, and dark to fake the shapes and sounds that guests take for the dead at work.

He prints how each feat is done, step by step. His aim is to save the crowd from fraud. The book is the stage's best word on the theme. Its scorn still stings.
hansard-suez-canal-shares-1876:
The House of Commons took up the Suez Canal share deal in its supply debate of February 14, 1876. Hansard holds the whole talk, word for word, in its record of that day. The deal had been struck in haste in the fall of 1875, with Rothschild cash.

The Prime Minister's men tell the House that the Rothschilds paid the Khedive near four million pounds at once. The price on the record is 3,976,582 pounds, with a fee of two and a half per cent. The debate is the chief first hand record of a deal that gave Britain a stake in Suez.
smith-chaldean-account-genesis-1876:
George Smith, a bank note engraver turned Assyriologist at the British Museum, wrote this book in 1876. He had taught himself to read the clay tablets of Babylon from the museum's vast store. Four years past, he had read out a flood tale from the tablets to a stunned London crowd.

The book sets the Babylonian tales of the making of the world and man by the side of Genesis. A flood tale far older than the Bible stands in its pages in clay writ form. The find shook the firm faith of Victorian Britain in the lone truth of its own text.
bonatti-astrologers-guide-1676:
Guido Bonatti was the most famed star man of the 1200s in Italy. His aphorisms, short sharp rules of the craft, came to England late. William Lilly turned them into English in 1676 as The Astrologer's Guide. The Latin name of the work is Anima Astrologiae.

One hundred and forty-six rules guide the star man in his work. They tell when a chart speaks true and when it lies. The rules draw on Arab craft passed down through Spain. The book forms a bridge from the old Arab art to the English school of Lilly.
twain-tom-sawyer-1876:
Mark Twain published The Adventures of Tom Sawyer in 1876, complete in the first edition text. The beloved Mississippi boyhood novel drew on Twain's own youth in Hannibal, Missouri, on the river. Its sunny mischief made Twain famous on both sides of the Atlantic at once.

Tom, raised by Aunt Polly, dodges school and chores for swimming, pirates, and treasure hunts. He whitewashes a fence by making the chore look like rare sport to his friends. At night he sees Injun Joe murder Dr. Robinson in the town graveyard in secret. Lost in a cave with Becky Thatcher, Tom finds both terror and buried gold there. The book's glow of boyhood hides sharp satire of village piety and pride.
perez-galdos-dona-perfecta-1876:
Benito Pérez Galdós published Doña Perfecta in 1876, here in Mary J. Serrano's English translation of 1895. Serrano's version, with a Howells introduction, gives Galdós's novel of provincial bigotry to English readers. Galdós, Spain's great realist, set old Spain against new in one benighted provincial town.

Pepe Rey, a young engineer, visits Orbajosa to wed his cousin Rosario and inspect his aunt's estate there. Doña Perfecta, his devout aunt, turns priest, town, and guerrilla band against the liberal intruder by degrees in secret. Rosario loves Pepe, but her mother's piety and the town's fanaticism close around the pair like walls. The close is murder, madness, and a lie agreed by all, in Galdós's coldest verdict on intolerance in Spain. Serrano and Howells presented the novel as Spain's answer to the great realists of Europe.
bradley-ethical-studies-1876:
F. H. Bradley published Ethical Studies in 1876, a set of essays on moral philosophy. Bradley attacks hedonism, the view that pleasure is the good, and Kantian duty done for duty's sake alone. Against both he sets self-realization: the self grows whole by taking its place in a moral community. My station and its duties is his famous phrase for that view.

Morality, he argues, lives in the customs and roles of a real society. Yet the self must also go beyond mere social rules toward an ideal. The book is the great statement of idealist ethics in English. It shaped welfare liberalism through readers like T. H. Green.
gibbon-decline-fall-vol-1-1776:
Edward Gibbon published Volume 1 of The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire in 1776. Gibbon tells the story of Rome from its height under the Antonines to the age of Constantine. Armies, emperors, frontiers, and the rise of Christianity fill the narrative. His irony and learning made the book an instant classic.

Famous chapters on early Christianity blamed the new faith in part for Rome's decay. Churchmen attacked him, and Gibbon replied with relish. The prose is stately, balanced, and often quietly mocking. Many call the History the greatest work of history in English. Volume 1 alone would secure Gibbon's fame.
taine-ancient-regime-durand-1876:
Hippolyte Taine's The Ancient Regime appears in John Durand's translation of 1876. The book opens Taine's Origins of Contemporary France, his study of the Revolution's causes. Taine applies his method of race, milieu, and moment to old France. Taxes, privilege, and a rigid central state crush the peasantry and starve reform.

He paints the court, the tax farmer, and the village in hard detail. The old regime, in his account, made revolution near certain. Taine wrote after the Paris Commune, and fear of crowds colors his work. Historians debate his science, yet respect his research. The volume is a classic of analytical history in the French style.
polano-talmud-selections-1876:
Polano's Talmud: Selections, published in 1876, offered English readers early and easy access to rabbinic literature. The Talmud itself is a vast record of Jewish law and debate in Hebrew and Aramaic. Polano chose and translated passages for a general audience.

The selections range over prayer, charity, family duty, court rulings, and tales of the rabbis at work. Readers could meet the Talmud's mix of strict law and warm story without facing its full bulk. The book served as an influential introduction for English readers curious about Jewish tradition. Victorian readers met a living tradition here, not a dead code.
coley-clavis-astrologiae-1676:
Henry Coley was a London astrologer and mathematician who succeeded William Lilly as the art's leading English teacher. His Clavis Astrologiae Elimata, published in 1676, is his complete textbook of astrology. The Latin title promises a key, filed smooth for the student's hand.

Coley teaches the casting of charts, the judgment of questions, and the reading of nativities in plain, ordered lessons. He trims Lilly's vast practice into rules a beginner can actually carry into a consultation. The Clavis served English astrologers as their standard manual into the next century. His almanacs kept his name before the public year after year.
proudhon-what-is-property-tucker-1876:
Benjamin R Tucker published his translation of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon's What is Property? in 1876. Proudhon, a French printer and self-taught thinker, had issued the memoir in 1840 and shocked France. His answer to his own question became famous at once: property is robbery.

Proudhon distinguished property, the right to use and abuse and charge rent, from simple possession of what one works. He attacked rent, interest, and profit taken without labor. Judges and economists denounced the book, and Proudhon answered them in later memoirs. The work is widely read as the founding text of anarchism, the first time a writer claimed that label with pride.
moliere-dramatic-works-vanlaun-vol4-1876:
Tartuffe, the most famous of all Molière's plays, leads volume four of van Laun's set, published in 1876. Tartuffe is a religious fraud who worms into a rich man's house and nearly steals all he owns. The play was banned for years in France for its daring.

Sharing the volume are Mélicerte, a pastoral piece left unfinished, and The Sicilian, a short musical comedy. Amphitryon retells the Greek myth of Jupiter wooing a mortal wife. George Dandin mocks a rich peasant who marries above his station and regrets it. Van Laun's notes trace how each play fared on the Paris stage.
moliere-dramatic-works-vanlaun-vol5-1876:
Volume five of van Laun's Molière, published in 1876, opens with The Miser. Harpagon, its grasping hero, loves his money box more than his own children. His greed drives the plot through loans, thefts, and crossed love affairs until the box itself is stolen.

The volume also gives Monsieur de Pourceaugnac, a farce about a country lawyer tormented in Paris. The Magnificent Lovers is a court spectacle in mythic dress. The Citizen Who Apes the Nobleman laughs at a rich tradesman hiring tutors to seem grand. Psyche, a grand verse tragedy with ballet, closes the volume in a very different key.
moliere-dramatic-works-vanlaun-vol6-1876:
Van Laun's sixth and last volume of Molière appeared in 1876 and holds the plays of his final years. The Rogueries of Scapin brings back the sly servant who beats his masters at their own game. The Learned Ladies satirizes women who prize book learning above sense, and men who flatter them.

The Imaginary Invalid, Molière's last play, mocks doctors and a hypochondriac who fears every ill. Tradition says Molière himself collapsed while playing that part and died soon after. The Countess of Escarbagnas and the early farces fill out the volume. With it, English readers gained the whole of Molière in one faithful set.
shi-king-book-of-poetry-legge-1876:
James Legge published his complete translation of the She King, the Book of Poetry, in 1876. It forms volume three of his Chinese Classics, in a revised edition with the Chinese text, prolegomena, and notes. The Shih Ching holds 305 songs and hymns, gathered in China more than two thousand years ago.

Court odes, temple hymns, and folk songs of love, harvest, and war stand side by side. Tradition credits Confucius with choosing and ordering the collection. Legge's prose renderings favor exact sense, while his notes carry the learning of Chinese commentators. The songs remain China's oldest poetry anthology and a school text for ages. English readers meet them whole in Legge.
ovid-fasti-tristia-ponto-riley-1876:
The later, sadder Ovid speaks in this volume of Henry T. Riley's Bohn prose translations. It gathers the Fasti, the Tristia, the Pontic Epistles, the Ibis, and the Halieuticon. Augustus exiled Ovid to Tomis on the Black Sea in 8 CE, and most of these poems plead from that cold shore.

The Fasti walks through the Roman year feast by feast, a poem of the calendar left half done. The Tristia and the letters from Pontus beg friends and the emperor for recall that never came. The Ibis curses an enemy, and the Halieuticon sings of fish. Riley's plain prose makes the exile books easy to follow.
bentham-theory-legislation-hildreth-1876:
Bentham's Theory of Legislation reached English readers through R. Hildreth's translation. Bentham himself never wrote the book in this form. His French editor Dumont built it from Bentham's manuscripts into a French redaction. Hildreth then carried that version into English for this edition.

Inside stands the utilitarian science of law: how to frame codes that raise happiness and cut pain. Civil and penal law both receive rules drawn from the one great principle. Legislators across Europe and Latin America studied the work for generations. It spread Bentham's name wider than his own tangled English prose could. The system here is clear, bold, and practical.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
Volume V of the Encyclopaedia of Pure Materia Medica appeared in 1876, the halfway point of Allen's ten. The symptoms of each remedy stand in strict anatomical order, a habit that lets a busy reader land on the right page fast. Sources are cited, so claims can be traced.

Some entries run for pages, proof of how often a drug was tested in that busy age of provings. Others stay brief. All of it feeds the same craft: choosing one remedy whose proved picture matches the sick person's signs. The volume keeps the archive's standard of full record over fine writing.
gill-myths-and-songs-from-the-south-paci:
William Wyatt Gill collected Myths and Songs from the South Pacific in 1876 from his years as a missionary in the Cook Islands. Mangaian traditions fill the volume: creation, the gods, and Avaiki, the underworld beneath the sea. Songs in native verse, Englished by Gill, carry the tales as the islanders themselves sang them.

Gill wrote down what elders told him before the old religion faded from living memory. Heroes, cannibal gods, and voyages of the soul pass in strange, splendid procession. The book remains a first source on Polynesian myth, gathered at the last moment it could be.
maxwell-matter-and-motion-1876:
Matter and Motion, published in 1876, is James Clerk Maxwell's short primer on the laws of moving bodies. Maxwell wrote it for beginners, not experts. In a few brief chapters he lays out the ground rules of Newtonian mechanics.

He covers space, time, velocity, force, and work, each defined with care. Worked examples show how the same laws govern a falling stone and a circling planet. Because Maxwell writes so clearly, the book became a model science primer, and students of physics still use it to meet the subject. Each short chapter builds on the last, so the logic stays easy to follow.
wallace-geographical-distribution-animal:
Alfred Russel Wallace, co-founder of the theory of evolution by natural selection, published the first volume of his Geographical Distribution of Animals in 1876. Wallace had spent years collecting in the Amazon and the Malay islands. He asked why each region holds the animals it does.

Volume One sets out the rules: how climate, seas, and land links shape where species can live. Wallace divides the world into six great regions, a scheme still in use. His maps and lists turned scattered facts into zoogeography, the study of animals across the map. Collectors and travelers supplied much of the raw data behind it.

Volume Two of Wallace's Geographical Distribution of Animals, also from 1876, puts his system to work region by region. Alfred Russel Wallace had catalogued thousands of species on his travels. Here he applies his rules to the lands of the Old World and beyond.

The volume works through Europe, Africa, Asia, and the islands of the Pacific in turn. For each region Wallace lists the families present and asks how they got there. Land bridges, past climates, and vanished seas all play a part. It completes the founding text of zoogeography. Readers meet the faunas of lands few had seen described before.
gray-darwiniana-1876:
Asa Gray was America's leading botanist and Darwin's chief ally across the Atlantic. His Darwiniana, from 1876, collects the essays and reviews he wrote as evolution fought for a hearing. Gray knew Darwin's work before most Americans did.

Gray explains natural selection in clear terms and answers its critics one by one. He also argues that faith and evolution need not clash, a view Darwin himself welcomed. The reviews trace the debate from the first shock of the Origin to wider acceptance. They show science being argued out in public, in real time. Gray wrote as both a working scientist and a man of faith.
plos-pone-0003376:
Nathan A. Baird and co-authors shared a cheaper way to map genes in this 2008 paper. Labs often track single-letter DNA changes, called SNPs, to build genetic maps. Good maps need many markers, and old ways to get them cost a lot. The team cut DNA at set points and read only the bits next to each cut.

Those short bits are called RAD markers, and each one can hold useful DNA changes. Reading them found many new markers and placed them on a map at once. The method is simple enough for species with few genetic tools. It opened genome mapping to far more kinds of plants and animals.
plos-pone-0003476:
Shuo Wang and co-authors traced a cancer control switch in this 2008 paper. A protein called p27 Kip1 restrains cell division. Losing that restraint is tied to many human cancers. The factor Stat1, key to immunity and tumor watch, acts in this pathway.

The team showed Stat1's phosphate state decides how Ras behaves. Ras is a growth signal that can turn cancerous. When Stat1 is set one way, it regulates p27 and checks Ras. The finding names a lever that helps decide tumor formation. Ras is among the most studied cancer genes in all of biology.
plos-pone-0003576:
Samir K. Saha and co-authors typed a meningitis germ without culture in this 2008 paper. Streptococcus pneumoniae causes pneumococcal meningitis, often in children. Standard serotyping needs the germ grown in culture first. Many patient samples come back culture negative.

Their sequential multiplex PCR approach named serotypes directly. It had not been applied where Asian serotypes are diverse. Naming the strain guides surveillance of disease patterns. It also informs which vaccines a region needs most. Meningitis kills fast, so a name for the strain must come within hours, not days. Serotypes also shift over time as vaccines press on them.
plos-pone-0003676:
Dorit Ben-Shachar and Rachel Karry published this psychiatry study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Faults in mitochondria, the cell's energy makers, have been reported in three major mental illnesses. The authors asked whether those faults look the same in schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depression.

They measured parts of mitochondrial complex I, the first step in the energy chain, across brain regions. The abnormal patterns differed by disease, each with its own map of affected areas. That contrast suggests the three disorders disturb energy metabolism in their own ways, not through one shared break.
plos-pone-0003776:
Demetrios Kalaitzidis and Benjamin G. Neel published this blood methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Hematopoietic stem cells are among the best-studied adult stem cells. Tools existed to read phosphoproteins in their offspring, but not in the rare stem cells themselves. The authors present a protocol to close that gap.

Using flow cytometry, they tracked protein phosphorylation in single stem and progenitor cells. Responses differed by the stimulus given and changed over time. The technique reveals how the blood system's root cells answer different calls, moment by moment. Rare cells like these are where blood diseases often begin.
plos-pone-0003876:
C. Jaco Klok and Jon F. Harrison tested how air oxygen shapes insect size in a 2009 PLOS ONE article. Fossil records link past swings in air oxygen with swings in insect body size. High oxygen seems to favor larger insects over long spans of time. The authors wanted a direct test of that link.

They bred the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster for large size under three oxygen levels. Low oxygen held back the gains that selection could make. The result supports the idea that thin air limits how big insects can grow. It helps explain why giant insects lived when air held more oxygen.
plos-pone-0003976:
Konrad U. Foerstner, Tobias Doerks, Jean Muller, and co-authors found an industrial enzyme in a eukaryote in 2008. Nitrile hydratases are bacterial enzymes used in industry and cleanup. They break down nitrile chemicals in wastewater. Computer screening searched many genomes for these enzymes.

Their PLOS ONE article reports one in Monosiga brevicollis, a single-celled eukaryote. Its two enzyme parts, usually separate, sit fused in one protein. A eukaryote copy widens the known spread of this enzyme family. It also hints at gene transfer between distant life forms. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004076:
Pablo Freire, Marco Vilela, Helena Deus, and co-authors explored DNA copy changes in a brain tumor in 2008. Glioblastoma multiforme is among the most lethal brain cancers. The Cancer Genome Atlas project began large-scale analysis of such tumors. It gathered genomic, expression, and clinical data together.

Their PLOS ONE article analyzes copy number alterations in glioblastoma samples. Gains and losses of DNA segments mark genes that drive growth. An exploratory pass shows patterns others can test in larger sets. The work demonstrates open analysis of shared cancer genome data. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004176:
Michael Tuvim and colleagues published this lung study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Influenza pneumonia kills many people every year, and pandemic flu has killed millions. Deaths have been blamed on a host response too weak to limit the virus. They have also been blamed on inflammation so strong that it damages the lung itself.

The team tested the second idea by boosting lung inflammation in advance. They report that augmented inflammation in the lung protects against influenza A pneumonia rather than worsening it. The result challenges the simple view that inflammation in flu is mostly harmful.
plos-pone-0004276:
Hirotaka Sakamoto and colleagues published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many men suffering from stress, including post-traumatic stress disorder, report sexual dysfunction, usually treated with counselling. The team had earlier identified a gastrin-releasing peptide system in the lumbar spinal cord that acts as a primary mediator of male sexual function.

Here they show that stress affects this spinal peptide system. The peptide is called GRP for short. The finding gives psychogenic erectile dysfunction a physical address in the spinal cord. A defined neural target could support treatments beyond counselling alone.
plos-pone-0004376:
Yeast cells give scientists a simple way to study basic cell survival. Laurence Vernis, Céline Facca, Emmanuelle Delagoutte, and co-authors worked with a mutant form of a yeast gene called TAH18. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper names a protein pair that the gene helps form. The pair is called the Dre2-Tah18 complex.

The authors report that this complex guards the cell's mitochondria, its energy-making parts. It also shapes whether a cell dies after oxidative stress, damage caused by reactive oxygen. The gene had first turned up in a screen for partners of a DNA-copying enzyme. Connecting it to mitochondria widens the story. Cell death control is central to much disease research.
plos-pone-0004476: In 2009, a team spotted touch points in fuzzy protein clumps well. Touch spots in low-detail protein clumps were guessed. The method found handshakes in blurry maps. The neat tool aids shape study greatly. The clumps are huge and highly complex.
plos-pone-0004576: In 2009, Gandhi, Zhang, and Xie linked lung-cancer gene glitches to drug response well. EGFR signaling pathway alterations and their relation to tyrosine kinase inhibitors were mapped. The mutations predicted TKI response. The finding guides targeted therapy. The cancers were NSCLC.
plos-pone-0004676: In 2009, Koella and a team explored a parasite fighting malaria from within here. A way to curb Plasmodium berghei in Anopheles mosquitoes was studied. The tiny parasite blocked malaria growth quite well. The finding aids biocontrol research. The exact way is unclear.
plos-pone-0004776: In 2009, Shapira, Katz, and Ali filmed mouse livers through tiny scopes anew. Murine laparoscopy enabled continuous in-vivo liver assessment across disease models. The tiny scopes tracked progression live. The handy tool aids hepatology research. The old strategies were flawed badly.
zola-his-excellency-1876:
Macmillan issued His Excellency in 1897 as the sole authorized English version, with Vizetelly's preface. Chapter heads run from The Corps Legislatif and Resignation to An Imperial Christening. Passion and Matrimony, In Retirement, and Recalled to Power follow in turn.

Eugene Rougon, the family's political genius, claws toward the top of the Second Empire. Minister and power broker, he masters the backroom deal and its price. Flatterers, mistresses, and favors traded like coin crowd around him. Zola dissects how power truly works with a razor edge. Few political novels match its grasp of influence, ambition, and the hunger that drives public men.
legge-the-shih-king-or-book-of-poetry-sh:
James Legge Englished China's oldest songbook in The Shih King, issued in 1876 with the Chinese text beside his version. Its 305 songs date from about the eleventh to the seventh century before Christ. Love songs, war songs, and harvest hymns all stand in its pages.

Legge, a Scottish scholar and missionary, gave Victorian readers a window on ancient China. Court odes praise kings, while folk ballads sing of longing and toil. The book formed part of the Sacred Books of the East series. Few anthologies anywhere are older or more loved, and this version pairs sound learning with the original words.
price-observations-civil-liberty-1776:
Price's Observations on the Nature of Civil Liberty appeared in 1776 and made him famous in a night. The dissenting minister wrote as Britain moved toward war with its American colonies. His pamphlet defended the American cause on principle, and it sold by the thousand in the year of independence.

Price defines liberty as self-government, for nations as for persons, and argues that Britain's claim to tax and bind the colonies was a form of slavery. He extends the argument to Ireland and India, which widened both the book's reach and its enemies. The government of the day considered prosecuting its author. The tract carried deep thought to the barricades across the sea, and it stands as the English voice of the American Revolution at its birth.
cia-0000009376:
Japan's strategic importance is spelled out in a CIA paper dated April 1948. Japan then sat under American occupation, three years after its defeat in the Second World War. Planners were deciding whether Japan would stay a ward or become an ally.

The paper weighs Japan's ports, industry, and position off the Asian mainland in Cold War terms. An anchored Japan guarded sea lanes and faced the Soviet Union across narrow waters. Judgments like this one fed the policy turn toward rebuilding Japan as a partner. The file shows that turn being reasoned out on paper.
cia-0000009676:
Six American prisoners were held at the Krong R'buk detention camp, a March 1971 item reports, in a Cambodian district the title cuts short. Detention camps in Cambodia's east held men captured as the war spread across the border in 1970. Conditions in such camps were rough and poorly documented.

Naming the camp and its count of Americans gave officials a concrete target for follow-up. Six men at one site could be checked against recent border losses. The report also shows captivity becoming a Cambodian story, not only a Vietnamese one. Its details preserve a camp that few outsiders ever saw.
cia-0000009876:
Four American prisoners were seen on May 15, 1968, walking north near a Laotian village. The title cuts the village name off at Ban Nath, and the report was filed that June. A precise date stands out in files where many sightings float undated. Walking north suggested movement toward central camps or toward Vietnam.

The second Adams report of 24 October 1862 is printed as Document 176 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain, sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Late October 1862 was a turning point in the war's foreign side: the French truce plan was taking shape, and Britain had to choose. Adams's twice-weekly reports were Washington's best window on that choice. This dispatch, read in sequence, shows the care with which he tracked each shift in British thinking. Adams held the London post from 1861 to 1868, the longest run of any Union envoy in Europe.
frus-1862-d276:
On 8 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William L. Dayton a dispatch printed as Document 276 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister to France, posted in Paris.

Early May brought word of the French defeat at Puebla and the Union hold on New Orleans, both useful to Washington's case in Paris. Seward's letters that month pressed a simple theme: the rebellion was failing, and friendship with it would cost France more than it could gain. This dispatch is one of the spring's many statements of that theme. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d376:
Viscount Treilhard wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 August 1862, in a letter printed as Document 376 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. He wrote on the second day of the Bull Run battle.

Few dates in the file carry such a charge: while Treilhard wrote, the Union army was being beaten thirty miles away. The defeat would embolden those in Europe who wanted to act on the war. This letter, and the exchange around it, belongs to the record of how Washington's foreign dealings absorbed the shock in real time. Seward tested what Mercier said against what Dayton reported from Paris, week by week.
frus-1862-d476:
On 13 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to James E. Harvey in Lisbon. It is Document 476 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

By October 1862 the Confederate cruiser Alabama was loose on the Atlantic. Neutral ports from the Azores outward had become part of the war at sea. Seward's autumn orders to Lisbon kept the pressure on Portugal to hold raiders to the letter of neutrality law. Harvey's post, quiet in most histories, sat on a real front of the war. The dispatch closes the year's printed instructions to Portugal, a small file that shows how global the blockade's paper war had become.
frus-1862-d576:
On 21 July 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to James Watson Webb in Brazil. The instruction is Document 576 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Seward's July orders everywhere carried the government's account of a hard summer, and the Brazilian instruction was no exception. Webb also needed the Department's current line on the cruiser war, since Confederate raiders would soon be working the South Atlantic and seeking Brazilian ports. By the time the letter reached Rio, the season it described had passed, which is why distant ministers held such wide discretion. The document shows the system working at its longest range.
frus-1862-d676:
Anson Burlingame sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 May 1862. Burlingame was the American minister to China, and his mail formed the China section of the year's file. The letter is document 676 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Spring reports from China dealt with the state of the ports and the mood of the Qing court. Burlingame also had to weigh the moves of Britain and France, whose fleets and envoys loomed large there. His letter is a working part of that watch. It helped Washington hold a steady course in East Asia with few ships and fewer men to spare.
frus-1863p1-d76:
Charles Francis Adams sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 12 February 1863. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 76 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Mid-February mail from London took stock after the opening of Parliament. Adams wrote on the tone of the houses, the press, and the South's men in the city. His reports let Seward judge whether the calm of the Queen's speech would hold. This dispatch is one of a pair sent that day, in the legation's usual split of topics.
frus-1863p1-d176:
On 30 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this dispatch from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 176 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Britain had declared itself neutral in 1861, yet many in its government and press leaned toward the South. Adams watched Parliament, the cabinet, and the newspapers for any sign of a shift. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d276:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 2 September 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 276 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Orders crossed the Atlantic by steamship and took ten days or more to arrive. By the time Adams acted, events in London could already have moved on. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d376:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, on 29 January 1863. The note is document 376 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Lyons reported everything to London, so Seward wrote knowing his words would be read there too. Each note spoke to two audiences at once. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d476:
On 23 April 1863 a formal note passed from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d576:
Under the date 22 June 1863, the record holds a letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d676:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, sent this dispatch to London on 24 November 1863. It went to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister there. The text is document 676 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that covers foreign affairs for 1863, part one.

Britain was the foreign power Washington watched most closely during the Civil War. Its ships, ports, and trade could help or hurt the Union cause. Adams had to press the American view in person, using notes like this one as his guide. The letter shows high-level orders moving from a desk in Washington to an envoy abroad, in plain official words.
plos-pbio-0020176:
Scott Makeig, Arnaud Delorme, Marissa Westerfield, and their team analyzed brain waves in PLOS Biology in 2004. They recorded scalp signals, called EEG, while people responded by hand to visual targets. The team broke the smooth EEG waves into sharper events tied to each response.

That finer view shows the brain's response as a set of brief bursts from distinct areas, not one slow wave. It changes how EEG data can be read and compared across studies. Brain-wave records are cheap and fast but blurry. Methods that sharpen them help labs link scalp signals to real events inside the brain. The timing is sharp, down to fractions of a second.
plos-pone-0000076:
Charles C. Carey, Kristen F. Gorman, and Suzannah Rutherford followed up on the Hsp90 buffer system in PLOS ONE in 2006. Hsp90 hides genetic variation by keeping flawed proteins working. The authors ask how that buffering is organized: whether it rests on one hub or spreads across connected parts, a property called modularity.

How the buffer is built decides how it fails. A modular buffer might release variation in one trait while holding the rest steady. That would make Hsp90 a finer tool for evolution than a simple on-off switch. The study refines the picture of a protein that many see as a capacitor for evolutionary change across species.
plos-pone-0000176:
Rebecca S. Levine, A. Townsend Peterson, Krista L. Yorita, and colleagues published this disease ecology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Monkeypox is a smallpox-like virus long present in forested parts of western and Central Africa. The authors map its ecological niche, the conditions where it occurs, to chart its geographic distribution across Africa.

Knowing where a zoonotic virus can live is the first step in predicting where it will strike. The authors model suitable habitat from known human cases. Their map guides surveillance toward the forests and climates where monkeypox is most likely to emerge.
plos-pone-0000276:
Reto Huber, Steve K. Esser, Fabio Ferrarelli, and colleagues published this sleep study in PLOS ONE in 2007. They used TMS, magnetic pulses through the skull, to boost activity in a patch of cortex while subjects were awake. The title reports the result: that local boost later increased slow wave activity, the deep-sleep brain rhythm, in the same area during sleep.

Slow waves are thought to reflect how much sleep pressure a brain region has built up. Showing that waking stimulation raises them locally supports the idea that sleep need is tracked region by region. The finding links daytime brain use to the depth of the following night's sleep.
plos-pone-0000376:
Spyridon Drosopoulos and colleagues tested what sleep does for memory, publishing in PLOS ONE in 2007. Remembering events in the right order is a basic part of memory: it matters whether the phone rang before or after the knock. The team asked whether sleep helps lock in that time order.

The study's title states its claim plainly: sleep enforces the temporal order in memory. Work like this supports a clear view of sleep. Sleep is not just rest but an active stage of memory building. During it, the brain sorts and firms up what was learned while awake. It speaks to students, shift workers, and anyone whose sleep is cut short.
plos-pone-0000476:
Nickolai A. Tchurikov and Olga V. Kretova used targeted gene silencing on a mobile DNA element in the fruit fly, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The element, called F, is a transposon-like sequence in Drosophila melanogaster that can move within the genome. Their method was suffix-specific RNAi, silencing aimed at a distinctive end region of the element's RNA.

Precise silencing matters because mobile elements share much of their sequence with each other and with normal genes. Hitting only the chosen target shows RNA interference can be aimed with fine resolution. Controlling mobile elements matters too, since their jumping can break genes and reshape genomes.
plos-pone-0000576:
Jean-Louis Boulay and colleagues reported a counterintuitive marker of brain tumor outcome, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. NOTCH2 is a gene in a signaling pathway that usually promotes growth. The team found that loss of NOTCH2 positively predicts survival in subgroups of human glial brain tumors: patients whose tumors lost it lived longer.

A marker that predicts survival helps doctors counsel patients and stratify trials, even before it suggests a treatment. The subgroup detail matters: gliomas are several diseases under one name, and a signal visible only in a subgroup would be missed in pooled data. The finding also hints that NOTCH2's growth role can cut the other way in these tumors.
plos-pone-0000676:
Henrik Bjørn Nielsen, John Mundy and Hanni Willenbrock offered a method for matching genes by how they respond, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Matching transcriptional responses across studies is a strong tool in functional genomics. A mutant, for example, can be described by matching its gene expression profile with profiles from other studies.

Their approach, FARO, stands for functional associations by response overlap. When two conditions move the same genes, they may share basic biology. Overlap in responses becomes a clue to function for genes whose role is still unknown. With expression data piling up in public archives, methods that mine overlaps turn old studies into new ideas.
plos-pone-0000776:
Zhen Xuan Yeo and colleagues modeled gene control as a sequence of logical steps, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cell signaling runs from a ligand binding a membrane receptor, through transcription factor activation, to induction of mRNA expression. The transcriptional-regulatory system plays a pivotal role in controlling gene expression, yet its dynamics over time are hard to follow from static data.

Their sequential logic model aims to decipher that dynamic control computationally. Step-by-step logic can simulate how a signal's timing shapes which genes turn on. Models of this kind let researchers test regulatory ideas cheaply before spending months on laboratory experiments.
plos-pone-0000876:
Rita Busuttil, Ana Maria Garcia, Robert Reddick and co-authors tracked how mutations build up with age inside mouse organs, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Earlier work with a special test mouse had shown changes pile up far faster in the small intestine than in the brain. The open question was how uneven that pattern is within a single organ.

Using the same model, the team compared sites inside the small intestine. They report that point mutations, single letter changes in DNA, do not land evenly. Uneven damage may help explain why some tissues age faster and face higher cancer risk. The study treats aging as a local process, not a uniform one.
plos-pone-0001076:
Jeremy Parker, Brian Bradley, Arne Mooers and colleagues reconstructed the family tree of the Nek kinases, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Neks are kinases tied to cilia and the cell cycle. In the fungus Aspergillus a single Nek is essential for cycle control. The ciliate Tetrahymena, by contrast, carries more than thirty.

That spread raises an evolutionary question: when did this family diversify. Their phylogenetic analysis reveals early diversification of the ciliary and cell cycle kinases. Cilia are ancient cell parts, and their kinases splitting early fits that age. The tree gives cell biologists a map for comparing Nek jobs across species.
plos-pone-0001176:
When proteins unfold, they tend to clump, and clumping ruins lab work and drug making alike. Utpal Das and colleagues examined how arginine, a widely used additive, stops that clumping, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Aggregation happens mainly when exposed water-hating surfaces on unfolded proteins bond.

The authors argue that supramolecular assemblies of arginine hold the key to its protective effect. Arginine is used everywhere as an aggregation suppressor, yet how it works stayed unclear. Their account of how arginine shields those sticky surfaces gives protein chemists a firmer basis for a routine trick.
plos-pone-0001276:
How wild birds pick up viruses, and pass them on, is mostly undocumented. Jaime Potti and colleagues traced one virus, an avian polyomavirus, through a wild songbird population, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Detailed patterns of primary virus acquisition and dispersal in wild vertebrates were virtually absent before such work.

The authors show that nestlings acquire polyomavirus infections from larval blowflies. These flies are common nest parasites of cavity-nesting birds. Breeding adults play a further role in spread. An insect parasite ferrying a bird virus is a transmission route few would have guessed. The study is a rare close-up of virus ecology in the wild.
plos-pone-0001376:
Eric Benner and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on Parkinson's disease, a brain ill that slowly kills nerve cells that make dopamine. Brains of patients show clumps of a changed protein inside nerve cells, plus signs of swelling in the tissue. The team asked how the immune response to that changed protein affects cell loss.

The authors report that immune action aimed at the changed protein speeds the death of dopamine nerve cells. That finding links the body's own defense to harm in this disease. It warns that shots or cures that stir this response must be used with care. The work adds a key piece to how Parkinson's grows worse.
plos-pone-0001476:
Margit Foss and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE caution on a cancer drug called Taxol. The drug binds and steadies the cell's inner rails, which blocks cell division. It had also been said to make the rails grow in new forms. The team asked whether some of those forms were in fact drug crystals.

They show that Taxol can form crystals that look much like steady rails under the scope. That likeness can fool even skilled eyes. Labs that study rail drugs must take care to split the two. The note saves others from building claims on a trick of the eye.
plos-pone-0001576:
Grit-Carsta Bulwin and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a brake signal for immune cells. A cell marker best known for showing germ parts to T cells was their focus. The team show one part of that marker can also send a brake signal. It does so by binding a partner on lymphocytes, the white cells that drive immune replies.

That brake cut swelling and pushed some lymphocytes to die, in dish tests and in mice. A built in brake on the same marker that starts replies is a neat design. Copying it could yield drugs for ills where immune replies run too hot.
plos-pone-0001676:
Richard A. Holland, Joseph L. Kirschvink, Thomas G. Doak, and their co-authors tested how bats sense the Earth's magnetic field in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Many animals use magnetic cues as a compass, but how any of them detects the field was unsettled. One proposed mechanism is light-based, as thought to work in birds. The other rests on magnetite, tiny magnetic mineral grains that could act as a built-in compass needle.

The authors' experiments support magnetite-based detection in bats, per the paper's title. The full text gives the behavioral tests, the magnetic pulses used to disturb magnetite, and how the bats' sense of direction changed. A magnetite compass in a mammal would show that nature evolved more than one way to read the planet's field.
plos-pone-0001776:
Tomokazu Fukuda, Yasuyuki Kondo, and Hitoshi Nakagama studied a tumor suppressor protein's parts in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The protein is CHFR, built from a forkhead-associated domain and a RING finger domain. CHFR is frequently switched off in human colon and gastric cancers, in up to half of cases, because its gene's promoter becomes methylated. That pattern suggests it normally suppresses tumors.

The team separated CHFR's jobs. Its anti-proliferative effects depend on the forkhead-associated domain, not on the E3 ligase activity of the RING finger. The full text gives the cell growth tests for each domain mutant. Knowing which part does the work focuses drug ideas on restoring that function.
plos-pone-0001876:
Kristopher Clark and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on two odd proteins, TRPM6 and TRPM7. Each one joins two jobs in a single chain. One part is a channel that lets charged atoms pass, and the other is a kinase that adds phosphate tags to proteins. How the kinase part is switched on and off was poorly known.

The team found that the kinase adds a great many tags to a rich stretch of its own chain, a process called autophosphorylation. They show that this self-tagging, on a scale they call massive, controls how active the kinase is. The result gives cell science a new lever for how these dual-role proteins are tuned.
plos-pone-0001976:
Jessica Jones-Carson and co-authors found how a host gas kills a dangerous bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The bacterium, Burkholderia mallei, causes glanders and resists many defenses. Much was unknown about how oxygen-based host defenses kill such a broad range of germs.

The team show that reactive nitrogen species, made by an enzyme that produces nitric oxide, account for the killing in their tests. As the title states, the attack works by inactivating the bacterium's iron-sulfur proteins, which are vital to its energy use. A clear kill step gives drug work a mechanism to mimic.
plos-pone-0002076:
Gisela Vaitaitis and David Wagner studied a rogue T cell group in autoimmune disease, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The pairing of CD40 on immune cells with its partner CD154 is critical in autoimmunity. A T cell group marked by CD40, called Th40 cells, harbors cells that attack the body's own tissue. In healthy people, that group is kept at contained levels.

The team found CD40 and a partner protein, TRAF2, packed at high levels in the raft domains of these cells' membranes. As the title states, that packing leads to preferential survival of this auto-aggressive group. A survival edge may be why such cells build up in illness.
plos-pone-0002176:
Ronald Miller, Nicolas Christoforou, Jonathan Pevsner, and co-authors searched for genes that build the heart, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Heart disease causes the largest share of adult death and illness in wealthy countries. Yet the gene programs that shape the early heart are still largely unknown. The team set out to find new cardiac genes in a systematic way.

They grew mouse embryonic stem cells and steered them toward heart cells, scanning gene activity with arrays as the cells changed. Genes that switched on along the way became candidates for roles in early heart formation. Each new gene on the list is a fresh lead for understanding birth defects of the heart.
plos-pone-0002276:
Amir Grosman and co-authors showed that a parasitic wasp turns its host into a bodyguard. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Many parasites and parasitoids change their host's behavior, and the changes are usually assumed to serve the parasite. Field tests of that idea are scarce, and it is often unclear whether host or parasite profits.

The team tested a parasitoid whose pupae develop outside the host caterpillar. The infected host is induced to guard the pupae and fight off predators, raising the pupae's survival. The field evidence shows a parasite pulling a host's strings for its own young's safety.
plos-pone-0002376:
Müller and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Martina Müller, Kerstin Fink, Julia Geisel, and others. Its subject is intestinal Colonization of IL-2 Deficient Mice with Non-Colitogenic B. vulgatus Prevents DC Maturation and T-Cell Polarization. IL-2 deficient (IL-2 −/−) mice mono-colonized with E.

coli mpk develop colitis whereas IL-2 −/− -mice mono-colonized with B. vulgatus mpk do not and are even protected from E. coli mpk induced colitis. We studied if mono-colonization with E. coli mpk or B. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002476:
Led by Dalmasso, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Guillaume Dalmasso, Hang Thi Thu Nguyen, Yutao Yan, and others. Its subject is butyrate Transcriptionally Enhances Peptide Transporter PepT1 Expression and Activity. PepT1, an intestinal epithelial apical di/tripeptide transporter, is normally expressed in the small intestine and induced in colon during chronic inflammation.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002576:
Research by Dusek and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Jeffery A. Dusek, Hasan H. Otu, Ann L. Wohlhueter, and others. Its subject is genomic Counter-Stress Changes Induced by the Relaxation Response. Mind-body practices that elicit the relaxation response (RR) have been used worldwide for millennia to prevent and treat disease.

The RR is characterized by decreased oxygen consumption, increased exhaled nitric oxide, and reduced psychological distress. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002676:
Work by Marion Coolen and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was molecular characterization of the gastrula in the turtle emys orbicularis : an evolutionary perspective on gastrulation. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Marion Coolen, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Due to the presence of a blastopore as in amphibians. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002776:
Work by Christian Gortázar and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was bovine tuberculosis in doñana biosphere reserve: the role of wild ungulates as disease reservoirs in the last iberian lynx strongholds. The catalog record names Christian Gortázar first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Doñana National Park (DNP) in southern Spain is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve where commercial hunting and wildlife artificial feeding do not take place and. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002876:
Simant Dube, Jian Qin and Ramesh Ramakrishnan presented a math method in PLOS ONE in 2008 for counting gene copies in a DNA sample. Copy number variation means stretches of the genome appear more or fewer times than usual, and such changes have been tied to disease. Their tool works with digital PCR run on a tiny fluid device.

The paper gives an algorithm the authors describe as sound in its math and fast to run. It turns raw device counts into an accurate copy number estimate. Labs that measure DNA dosage for research or diagnosis get a clearer way to handle the numbers these small devices produce.
plos-pone-0002976:
Joel Baumgart, Iuliia Vitko, Isabelle Bidaud and co-authors studied a loop inside low-voltage calcium channels in 2008. Calcium and sodium channels are built from four linked repeats, joined by inner loops with key regulatory roles. The loop joining repeats I and II matters greatly in high-voltage channels.

Here the focus is the same loop in low-voltage-activated channels, which govern rhythmic firing in brain and heart. The team identified structural parts of the loop that control gating and surface expression. Published in PLOS ONE, the detail aids design of drugs that target these channels. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003076:
Laura Reed, Brooke LaFlamme and Therese Markow studied hybrid male sterility in fruit flies in 2008. The genetic basis of postzygotic isolation is a central puzzle in evolutionary biology. Forces causing hybrid sterility act on the responsible genes while they are still varying within species, so the traits must be studied as they arise.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team analyzes intraspecies variation for interspecies isolation. That design catches sterility genes mid-process, before species fully split. The work helps explain how two populations become unable to breed, a core step in the origin of species.
plos-pone-0003176:
David M. Paterson, Rebecca J. Aspden, Pieter T. Visscher and colleagues study living sediment mats in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. For the first time, they studied the power of stromatolite microbial groups to act as natural ecosystem engineers. Stromatolites are layered structures formed by microbial activity. They are thought to have ruled the shallows of the early oceans.

The team test light-dependent biostabilisation, the way these mats hold sediments together, and how it depends on light. Readers see ancient-style microbe groups doing work that can be measured in modern settings. The study links early Earth life to present coastal processes in a direct way, through tests.
plos-pone-0003276:
Shin-ichi Todoroki studies a destructive fibre phenomenon in this single-author 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Fiber fuse is a process of optical fiber destruction under the action of laser radiation, found twenty years earlier. Once initiated, optical discharge runs along the fiber core region toward the light source and leaves periodic voids whose shape looks like a bullet pointing in the direction of travel.

The author observes in situ the modulated light emission of fiber fuse synchronized with the void train over a hetero-core splice point. Readers get a close look at a failure mode that can destroy communication lines. Understanding the fuse may help design fibres or sensors that resist it.
plos-pone-0007376: Scientists tested acridine-based chemicals, already known to work against prion proteins, against a plant RNA virus used as a lab stand-in for how RNA viruses copy themselves. They tracked whether the compounds blocked the virus from gathering and copying its genetic material. Blocking these steps is valuable both for learning how viruses grow and for finding leads toward new antiviral drugs.
plos-pone-0007476: The brain's support cells, astrocytes, keep their own daily rhythm. This study found that mouse and rat astrocytes show circadian swings in gene activity — the internal clock still ticks — but their uptake of the chemical messenger glutamate stays constant around the clock. The split shows the clock controls some astrocyte jobs but not others.
plos-pone-0007576: Fruit fly embryos develop reliably even as temperatures swing — a robustness this study traces to the endo-siRNA pathway. Disrupting that small-RNA system made development fragile to natural temperature shifts. The finding reveals a hidden stabilizer that keeps embryos on track through a changing world.
plos-pone-0007676: Some genes modify the severity of inherited diseases, and SAA1 is one of the few proven modifiers in humans — it influences kidney risk in familial Mediterranean fever. This study shows the modifier gene itself is subject to negative selection. The finding reveals evolution pruning a gene that shapes another disease.
plos-pone-0007776: Flu's toll in the tropics is poorly measured. This study tracked influenza pneumonia in Thailand from 2005 to 2008, recording incidence, seasonality, and deaths. The multi-year data give subtropical countries the evidence base for vaccine policy.
plos-pone-0007876: St. Louis encephalitis virus once caused America's worst mosquito-borne brain outbreaks. This study passaged the virus through mosquitoes and chickens to reveal its evolutionary traits. The experiments explain why SLEV faded as West Nile rose.
plos-pone-0007976: Anopheles funestus spreads malaria across Africa, yet its genetics lag behind its cousin An. gambiae. This study compared the global gene activity of mosquitoes from Mali. The transcriptome lays groundwork for the species' genome and new control strategies.
plos-pone-0008076: Cells were shown to fight bacterial pores with phosphatases. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Aguilar and colleagues found that phosphatase-dependent regulation tunes epithelial MAPK responses to toxin-induced membrane pores. Pore-forming toxins punch holes in cells, and MAPK alarms ring. The phosphatase control reveals how cells calibrate their counterattack.
plos-pone-0008176: A dangerous germ's full protein set was counted. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Becher's team pushed toward quantifying the entire Staphylococcus aureus proteome. The genome is the blueprint, but proteins do the actual work of the living cell. Because bacteria are simply built, they are ideal for a complete parts list. The proteomic push shows how close science has come to cataloging every protein in this major human pathogen.
plos-pone-0008276: Most new African HIV infections were traced to faithful couples. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Guthrie's team studied sexually transmitted infections among HIV-discordant couples. When one partner has HIV, other infections may raise transmission odds. The couple-focused data reframe prevention. The findings push protection where most infections actually happen.
